Chronic Kidney Disease.explanation: Uremic pericarditis (with characteristic scratching friction rub) and arrhythmias (from hyperkalaemia and electrolyte disturbances) are the most characteristic uremic manifestations. Pulmonary oedema and heart failure may occur secondary to volume overload or hypertension but are not defining uremic findings.

Chronic Kidney Disease.question: Which are nephroprotective? 1. ACE inhibitors  2. ARBs  3. Acetaminophen  4. β-blockers
Chronic Kidney Disease.explanation: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are nephroprotective: they reduce efferent arteriolar resistance, lower intraglomerular pressure, decrease proteinuria and slow CKD progression. Acetaminophen (safer than NSAIDs) and β-blockers provide no independent nephroprotection.

Chronic Kidney Disease.question: True about uremia: 1. Anemia  2. Hyperphosphatemia  3. Uremic frost  4. Hyperkalemia
Chronic Kidney Disease.explanation: All four are true of uraemia: normocytic anaemia (reduced EPO), hyperphosphataemia (impaired renal excretion), uremic frost (urea crystal deposition on skin in severe untreated uraemia) and hyperkalaemia (reduced K⁺ excretion). All are classic findings in advanced CKD.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Nephrotic syndrome typically presents with: 1. Hypoalbuminemia  2. Hypercholesterolemia  3. Edema  4. Tubular proteinuria
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: The classic triad of nephrotic syndrome is heavy glomerular proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia and oedema, accompanied by hypercholesterolaemia (from increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis). Tubular proteinuria occurs in tubulointerstitial disease, not nephrotic syndrome.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Which of the following are presented by nephrotic syndrome? 1. Membranous GN  2. Chronic pyelonephritis  3. Diabetic nephropathy  4. AL amyloidosis
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Membranous GN, diabetic nephropathy and AL amyloidosis all cause heavy glomerular proteinuria leading to nephrotic syndrome. Chronic pyelonephritis is a tubulointerstitial disease causing mild proteinuria and progressive CKD — it does not produce nephrotic syndrome.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Which of the following are presented by nephrotic syndrome? 1. Membranous GN  2. Chronic pyelonephritis  3. Diabetic nephropathy  4. AA amyloidosis
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Membranous GN, diabetic nephropathy and AA amyloidosis all cause nephrotic-range proteinuria. Chronic pyelonephritis is tubulointerstitial and does not cause nephrotic syndrome.

Glomerular Diseases.question: All of the following are presented by nephritic syndrome but one:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Membranoproliferative GN, mesangioproliferative GN and IgA nephropathy all present with a nephritic pattern (haematuria, RBC casts, hypertension, reduced GFR). AA amyloidosis characteristically presents with nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria) rather than a nephritic picture.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Microalbuminuria means ….. per 24-hour albumin (mg/24 h):
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Microalbuminuria (now termed 'moderately increased albuminuria') is defined as 30–300 mg albumin/24 h. Below 30 mg/24 h is normal; above 300 mg/24 h is macroalbuminuria. It is an early marker of glomerular injury in diabetes and hypertension.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Increased titers of which antibodies can help confirm the diagnosis of poststreptococcal GN? 1. Antistrepto-DNase  2. Anti-glomerular basement membrane  3. Antiphospholipid  4. Antistreptohyaluronidase
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Anti-DNase B and antistreptohyaluronidase confirm recent Group A streptococcal infection and support the diagnosis of PSGN. Anti-GBM antibodies are seen in Goodpasture syndrome; antiphospholipid antibodies in antiphospholipid syndrome — neither are relevant to PSGN.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Which of the following syndromes is the classic presentation of poststreptococcal GN?
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: PSGN classically presents as acute nephritic syndrome: haematuria (cola-coloured urine), RBC casts, mild-to-moderate proteinuria, oedema, hypertension and reduced GFR. Fanconi syndrome is a proximal tubular disorder; anti-GBM disease is a separate entity.

Glomerular Diseases.question: All of the following are characteristics of poststreptococcal GN, EXCEPT:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: PSGN is an immune-mediated disease presenting with haematuria, oedema and hypertension. Bacteriuria is not a feature — the urine sediment shows RBCs and RBC casts, not bacteria, because there is no active urinary infection.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Treatment of poststreptococcal GN must include:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Management of PSGN is primarily supportive (antihypertensives, diuretics). Antibiotics (e.g. penicillin) are given to eradicate residual streptococcal infection. Glucocorticoids, cytotoxics and thrombolytics are not indicated as PSGN is typically self-limited.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Which examination can clarify the location of immune deposits and the status of the glomerular basement membrane?
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Electron microscopy is the only modality that localises immune complex deposits (subepithelial, subendothelial, mesangial), assesses GBM structural integrity, and detects podocyte foot process effacement. CT and angiography are radiological tools evaluating anatomy and vasculature, not ultrastructure.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Podocyte abnormalities with genetic mutations lead to:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Mutations in podocyte/slit-diaphragm genes (NPHS1-nephrin, NPHS2-podocin, ACTN4, TRPC6, INF2) disrupt the glomerular filtration barrier causing hereditary/familial FSGS and steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. Membranous GN is autoimmune (anti-PLA2R) and pyelonephritis is tubulointerstitial.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Causes of secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis: 1. Pamidronate  2. Sickle cell disease  3. Hypertensive nephropathy  4. Cholesterol emboli
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: All four cause secondary FSGS: pamidronate causes direct podocyte toxicity; sickle cell disease causes hyperfiltration injury; hypertensive nephropathy produces adaptive glomerulosclerosis; cholesterol emboli cause ischaemic glomerular injury with segmental sclerosis.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Treatment of secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis must include: 1. Treatment of underlying cause  2. Control of proteinuria  3. Glucocorticosteroid  4. Immunosuppressive agent
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Secondary FSGS is structural/adaptive, not immune-mediated. Treatment targets the underlying cause (e.g. stopping pamidronate, treating obesity) and controlling proteinuria with ACE inhibitors/ARBs and blood pressure management. Glucocorticoids and immunosuppressives are not indicated unless an immune-mediated process co-exists.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Which of the following is first-line therapy for minimal change disease?
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Minimal change disease (podocyte foot process effacement on EM, normal LM) is the most common nephrotic syndrome in children. First-line therapy is glucocorticoids (prednisone), which induce remission in the majority. Enalapril is supportive; aspirin and fraxiparin are not treatments for MCD.

Glomerular Diseases.question: All are features of membranous GN, except:
options: Diffuse granular deposits of IgG and C3
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Membranous nephropathy is a cause of nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema). Characteristic IF shows diffuse granular IgG/C3 along the GBM. It does NOT present as nephritic syndrome (haematuria, RBC casts, acute GFR drop) — that pattern is seen in PSGN or rapidly progressive GN.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Treatment of membranous glomerulonephritis involves: 1. Edema control  2. Control of hypertension  3. Renin–angiotensin system inhibition  4. Dyslipidemia control
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Comprehensive supportive care for nephrotic syndrome is essential: loop diuretics for oedema, strict BP control, ACE inhibitors/ARBs to reduce intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria, and statins for nephrotic-related hyperlipidaemia and cardiovascular risk. All four are required regardless of immunosuppression decisions.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Causes of secondary membranous glomerulonephritis: 1. Infection  2. Drugs  3. Autoimmune diseases  4. Cancer
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Secondary membranous GN is caused by infections (HBV, HCV, syphilis), drugs (NSAIDs, gold, penicillamine), autoimmune diseases (SLE class V, other CTDs) and malignancies (solid tumours, haematological). All must be excluded before diagnosing primary membranous nephropathy.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Causes of secondary membranous glomerulonephritis (autoimmune): 1. Systemic lupus erythematosus  2. Rheumatoid arthritis  3. Sjögren's syndrome  4. Primary biliary cirrhosis
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: SLE (class V lupus nephritis), rheumatoid arthritis (also via gold/penicillamine therapy), Sjögren's syndrome and primary biliary cirrhosis are all recognised autoimmune causes of secondary membranous GN.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Complications of membranous GN: 1. CKD  2. Renal vein thrombosis  3. Pulmonary embolism  4. Deep venous thrombosis
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Membranous GN has one of the highest thromboembolic risks among nephrotic syndromes due to urinary loss of antithrombin III and other anticoagulants. Renal vein thrombosis, DVT and PE are all recognised complications. Progressive CKD also occurs in a significant proportion of patients.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Glomerulonephritis — which of the following are presented by nephrotic syndrome? 1. Membranous GN  2. Chronic pyelonephritis  3. Diabetic nephropathy  4. AL amyloidosis
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Membranous GN, diabetic nephropathy and AL amyloidosis cause glomerular proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome. Chronic pyelonephritis is tubulointerstitial and does not produce nephrotic syndrome.

Glomerular Diseases.question: In women with symptoms of acute cystitis, minimal bacterial colony count threshold is more than … bacteria/mL:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: In symptomatic women with acute uncomplicated cystitis, ≥10³ CFU/mL of a uropathogen is diagnostically significant. The traditional ≥10⁵ CFU/mL threshold applies to asymptomatic bacteriuria; lower counts are clinically meaningful when symptoms are present.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Which of the following is presented by nephritic syndrome?
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Mesangioproliferative GN presents with haematuria and nephritic features. Aβ amyloidosis typically presents with nephrotic syndrome; AANF amyloidosis is localised to the cardiac atria; AA amyloidosis usually presents with nephrotic syndrome.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Nephrotic syndrome classically presents with: 1. Hypoalbuminemia  2. Hypercholesterolemia  3. Edema  4. Mild proteinuria
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome presents with heavy (not mild) glomerular proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hypercholesterolaemia. Mild proteinuria is incorrect — the defining feature is nephrotic-range (>3.5 g/day) proteinuria.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Types of proteinuria: 1. Selective  2. Nonselective  3. Orthostatic  4. Functional
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: The standard classification includes selective (predominantly albumin, e.g. minimal change disease), nonselective (multiple proteins of varying size, e.g. membranous GN), and orthostatic (benign, occurs when upright, common in adolescents). 'Functional' is not an established principal category in this classification.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Causes of transient proteinuria: 1. Obesity  2. Nephrotic syndrome  3. Congestive heart failure  4. Nephritic syndrome
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Transient proteinuria is reversible and haemodynamic. Obesity (hyperfiltration) and CHF (renal venous congestion) both cause it. Nephrotic and nephritic syndrome produce persistent proteinuria from structural glomerular damage — not transient.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Causes of transient proteinuria: 1. Sleep apnea  2. Fever  3. CHF  4. Ascites
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: All four cause transient (functional) proteinuria: sleep apnoea (intermittent hypoxia/intrathoracic pressure changes), fever (altered glomerular permeability), CHF (venous congestion and haemodynamic changes) and ascites (altered intravascular volume).

Glomerular Diseases.question: Causes of transient proteinuria: 1. Emotional stress  2. Nephritic syndrome  3. Nephrotic syndrome  4. Congestive heart failure
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Emotional stress (transient glomerular permeability change) and CHF (haemodynamic) cause transient proteinuria. Nephritic and nephrotic syndromes are associated with persistent proteinuria from structural glomerular inflammation or damage.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Which of the following are presented by nephrotic syndrome? 1. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis  2. Membranous GN  3. AL amyloidosis  4. AA amyloidosis
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: All four cause nephrotic syndrome: FSGS (major cause in adults and children), membranous GN (classic adult nephrotic), AL amyloidosis (glomerular light-chain deposition) and AA amyloidosis (glomerular amyloid deposition causing nephrotic-range proteinuria).

Glomerular Diseases.question: All are characteristic of minimal change disease, except:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome with massive oedema, selective proteinuria (predominantly albumin) and severe hyperlipidaemia. Absence of oedema is incorrect — oedema is a prominent and expected feature.

Glomerular Diseases.question: All are characteristics of minimal change disease, except:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: MCD presents with massive oedema, severe hypoalbuminaemia and heavy proteinuria as part of nephrotic syndrome. The urine sediment is bland (acellular) — absence of RBC casts and inflammatory cells distinguishes MCD from nephritic processes. Cellular urine sediment is therefore NOT a feature of MCD.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Causes of secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis: 1. Analgesics  2. Radiation nephritis  3. Alport's syndrome  4. Heroin
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: All four cause secondary FSGS: chronic analgesic nephropathy (nephron loss → hyperfiltration → FSGS), radiation nephritis (vascular/parenchymal injury → sclerosis), Alport's syndrome (hereditary GBM defect → progressive glomerular injury) and heroin-associated nephropathy (classically linked to FSGS).

Glomerular Diseases.question: Characteristic of poststreptococcal GN: 1. Hematuria  2. Bacteriuria  3. Edema  4. Hypertension
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: PSGN presents as acute nephritic syndrome: haematuria (often gross, cola-coloured), oedema and hypertension from sodium/water retention. Bacteriuria is NOT a feature — PSGN is immune-mediated, not an active UTI; urine sediment shows RBCs/RBC casts, not bacteria.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Increased titers of which antibodies can help confirm the diagnosis of poststreptococcal GN? 1. Antistrepto-DNase  2. Anti-glomerular basement membrane  3. Antiphospholipid  4. Antistreptohyaluronidase
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Antistreptohyaluronidase (option 4) confirms recent streptococcal infection and supports PSGN diagnosis. Anti-GBM antibodies are characteristic of Goodpasture syndrome; antiphospholipid antibodies of antiphospholipid syndrome — neither is relevant to PSGN. (Note: Anti-DNase B is also a valid streptococcal antibody but was not included as a selectable correct answer in this version of the question.)

Glomerular Diseases.question: Which syndrome is the classic presentation of poststreptococcal GN?
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: PSGN classically presents as acute nephritic syndrome: haematuria (cola-coloured urine with RBC casts), mild-to-moderate proteinuria, oedema, hypertension and reduced GFR. Fanconi syndrome is a proximal tubular disorder; anti-GBM and glomerular vascular are not recognised clinical syndrome names.

Glomerular Diseases.question: All of the following are potent to induce membranous GN, except:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: NSAIDs (including ibuprofen) and penicillamine are well-recognised causes of drug-induced membranous GN. Infliximab (anti-TNF-α) is used to treat autoimmune conditions and is not a classic trigger of membranous nephropathy.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Vesicoureteral reflux is common among: 1. Advanced age population  2. Patients with intestinal disorders  3. Patients with severe cough  4. Patients with anatomic abnormalities of urinary tract
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: VUR results from incompetence of the ureterovesical junction, typically due to congenital structural abnormalities (short intramural ureter, dysfunctional insertion). It is most common in children, not the elderly. Intestinal disorders and severe cough are not causes.

Glomerular Diseases.question: True about nephrotic syndrome: 1. Hypoalbuminemia  2. Hypocholesterolemia  3. Edema  4. Tubular proteinuria
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome features hypoalbuminemia (heavy urinary albumin loss) and oedema (reduced oncotic pressure and sodium retention). It causes HYPERcholesterolaemia (not hypo-), from increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis. Proteinuria is glomerular (not tubular) in origin.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Seen in nephritic syndrome: 1. Proteinuria >3.5 g/24 h  2. Hematuria  3. Pyuria  4. Proteinuria <3 g/24 h
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Nephritic syndrome is characterised by haematuria (often with RBC casts), pyuria (from glomerular inflammation), and mild-to-moderate proteinuria typically <3–3.5 g/24 h. Proteinuria >3.5 g/24 h is the threshold for nephrotic syndrome, not nephritic.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Subepithelial 'humps' on biopsy are characteristic of:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Subepithelial 'humps' on electron microscopy represent subepithelial immune complex deposits and are a pathognomonic finding of postinfectious (classically poststreptococcal) GN. AL and AA amyloidosis show Congo red-positive amyloid deposits; FSGS shows segmental sclerosis without immune complex humps.

Glomerular Diseases.question: True about poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: PSGN is primarily self-limited and managed supportively. Immunosuppression is not routinely indicated. Antibiotics ARE indicated to eradicate residual streptococcal infection. Complement C3 levels are DECREASED (consumed by immune complex activation), not increased.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Flank pain in acute poststreptococcal GN is due to:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: In PSGN, diffuse glomerular inflammation causes renal swelling and enlargement, which stretches the innervated renal capsule producing flank pain. Hypertension causes headache; microhaematuria and proteinuria do not directly cause flank pain.

Glomerular Diseases.question: True about poststreptococcal nephritis: 1. ↓ Serum complement (C3)  2. Immune-mediated disease  3. History of skin/throat infection  4. Flank pain
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: All four are true of PSGN: C3 is reduced (complement consumption by immune complexes); it is immune complex-mediated; it follows streptococcal pharyngitis or impetigo by 1–3 weeks; and flank pain occurs from renal enlargement and capsular stretching.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Which markers help in diagnosis of poststreptococcal nephritis? 1. Anti-GBM  2. Anti-streptococcal antibodies  3. Anti-DNase B  4. Anti-hyaluronidase antibodies
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Anti-streptococcal antibodies, anti-DNase B (particularly useful after skin infections) and anti-hyaluronidase confirm recent streptococcal infection and support the PSGN diagnosis. Anti-GBM antibodies are characteristic of Goodpasture syndrome, not PSGN.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Nephrotic syndrome presents with: 1. Heavy proteinuria  2. Hypercholesterolemia  3. Hypoalbuminemia  4. ↑ Plasma creatinine level
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: The classic triad of nephrotic syndrome is heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/24 h), hypoalbuminaemia (from urinary protein loss) and hypercholesterolaemia (increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis). Elevated plasma creatinine may develop but is not a defining diagnostic criterion — GFR may be normal initially.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Nephrotic syndrome classically presents with: 1. Hypoalbuminemia  2. Hypercholesterolemia  3. Edema  4. Heavy proteinuria
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: All four are cardinal features of nephrotic syndrome: hypoalbuminaemia (urinary albumin loss), hypercholesterolaemia (compensatory hepatic lipoprotein synthesis), oedema (reduced oncotic pressure) and heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/24 h, the defining feature).

Glomerular Diseases.question: Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in elderly patients:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Membranous glomerulonephritis (membranous nephropathy) is the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults and particularly the elderly, where it may be primary (anti-PLA2R) or secondary to malignancy, autoimmune disease or drugs. Minimal change disease predominates in children. Analgesic nephropathy and pyelonephritis are tubulointerstitial diseases.

Glomerular Diseases.question: True about treatment of minimal change disease: 1. Prednisone  2. Cyclophosphamide  3. Cyclosporine  4. Mycophenolate mofetil
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: All four are used in MCD: prednisone is first-line (most patients respond); cyclophosphamide for frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent disease; cyclosporine for steroid-resistant/dependent disease; mycophenolate mofetil as a steroid-sparing agent. The choice depends on the clinical course.

Glomerular Diseases.question: FSGS — correct features: 1. Hematuria  2. Hypertension  3. Proteinuria  4. Renal calculi
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: FSGS typically presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension (common in progressive disease) and microscopic haematuria. Renal calculi are not a feature of FSGS.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Causes of FSGS: 1. Analgesic nephropathy  2. Reflux nephropathy  3. Pamidronate  4. Oligomeganephronia
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: All four cause secondary FSGS: analgesic nephropathy (nephron loss → hyperfiltration), reflux nephropathy (nephron loss → adaptive hyperfiltration), pamidronate (collapsing FSGS from podocyte toxicity) and oligomeganephronia (congenital reduced nephron number → hyperfiltration injury).

Glomerular Diseases.question: Urine sediment finding indicating GN: 1. RBC casts  2. Bacteriuria  3. Dysmorphic RBCs  4. Glucosuria
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: RBC casts (RBCs trapped in Tamm-Horsfall protein within tubules) and dysmorphic RBCs (deformed by passage through damaged GBM) are both highly specific for glomerular disease. Bacteriuria indicates UTI; glucosuria indicates diabetes or tubular dysfunction — neither indicates GN.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Microscopic hematuria — exclude: 1. Renal stone  2. Renal vascular injury  3. Benign prostatic hypertrophy  4. Interstitial nephritis
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Renal stones, renal vascular injury and BPH are all common causes of microscopic haematuria that must be excluded. Interstitial nephritis typically presents with pyuria, eosinophiluria and mild proteinuria — haematuria is not a primary finding and need not be excluded for it.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Treatment of ANCA small vessel vasculitis includes: 1. Tonsillectomy  2. Plasmapheresis  3. Methylprednisolone  4. Cyclophosphamide
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA, MPA) is treated with plasmapheresis (severe RPGN or pulmonary haemorrhage), high-dose IV methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide (or rituximab) as induction therapy. Tonsillectomy is not part of standard management.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Range of proteinuria in Wegener's granulomatosis is …… g/24 h:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: In granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's), renal involvement produces rapidly progressive GN with subnephrotic proteinuria, typically 0.5–1 g/24 h. Nephrotic-range proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) is uncommon and suggests an alternative or overlapping glomerular process.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Seen in Wegener's granulomatosis: 1. Hemoptysis  2. Macrohematuria  3. Microhematuria  4. Shortness of breath
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: GPA (Wegener's) typically causes haemoptysis (pulmonary capillaritis/alveolar haemorrhage), microhaematuria (pauci-immune GN) and dyspnoea (pulmonary infiltrates). Macrohematuria (gross haematuria) is uncommon — renal involvement usually produces only microscopic haematuria.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Vesicoureteral reflux is common among: 1. Advanced age population  2. Patients with intestinal disorders  3. Patients with severe cough  4. Patients with anatomic abnormalities of urinary tract
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: VUR is most strongly associated with anatomic abnormalities of the ureterovesical junction (congenital), intestinal disorders (constipation/dysfunctional elimination increasing bladder pressure) and severe cough (repeated intra-abdominal pressure surges). VUR is predominantly a paediatric condition — advanced age alone is not a risk factor.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Characteristic of IgA nephropathy: 1. Hematuria during upper respiratory infection  2. Hematuria immediately after upper respiratory infection  3. Episodic hematuria  4. Nephrotic syndrome is uncommon
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) causes synpharyngitic haematuria — appearing concurrently with or within 1–2 days of a URI (not after a latent period). Episodic gross haematuria is typical, and nephrotic syndrome is uncommon. Haematuria 1–3 weeks AFTER infection is the pattern of poststreptococcal GN.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Typical of IgA nephropathy: 1. Hematuria  2. IgA mesangial deposition  3. Male predominance  4. Peak incidence in fifth decade
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: IgA nephropathy presents with recurrent haematuria (synpharyngitic), mesangial IgA deposition (defining histological feature) and clear male predominance (~2–3:1). Peak incidence is in the second and third decades, not the fifth.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Causes of secondary membranous glomerulonephritis: 1. Colon cancer  2. Hepatitis B  3. SLE  4. NSAIDs
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: All four are recognised causes of secondary membranous GN: malignancies (especially colon, lung, breast), hepatitis B (infection-related), SLE class V (lupus nephritis) and NSAIDs (drug-induced). All must be excluded before diagnosing primary membranous nephropathy.

Glomerular Diseases.question: True about nephrotic syndrome: 1. Transient proteinuria  2. IgG deficiency  3. Edema formation  4. Antithrombin deficiency
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome causes urinary loss of IgG (predisposing to infection), oedema (hypoalbuminaemia + sodium retention) and antithrombin III deficiency (lost in urine, causing hypercoagulability). Proteinuria in nephrotic syndrome is persistent and heavy (>3.5 g/day), NOT transient.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Classic features of acute nephritic syndrome: 1. Edema  2. Hypertension  3. Hematuria  4. RBC casts
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: All four are classic features: oedema (sodium/water retention), hypertension (volume expansion and reduced GFR), haematuria (typically gross cola-coloured or microscopic) and RBC casts (pathognomonic of glomerular bleeding). Together they define the acute nephritic picture.

Glomerular Diseases.question: For which substances is crossing of the glomerular wall normally prevented by charge selectivity? 1. Albumin  2. Globulins  3. High-molecular-weight proteins  4. IgG
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: The glomerular filtration barrier uses both size and charge selectivity. Albumin, globulins and IgG are negatively charged and are primarily repelled by the negative charge of the GBM and podocyte slit diaphragm. High-molecular-weight proteins are excluded mainly by size selectivity, not charge alone.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Minimal change disease causes:
options: Fusion of glomerular epithelial cell foot processes
Loss of negative charge of the GBM
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: The pathognomonic finding in minimal change disease is diffuse effacement (fusion) of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy. Light microscopy is normal and immunofluorescence is negative. It is a primary podocyte disorder — tubular changes are not the primary pathology.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Poststreptococcal GN develops …… weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: PSGN develops 1–3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis (or 3–6 weeks after skin infection/impetigo). This latency period reflects the time for immune complex formation and glomerular deposition. IgA nephropathy occurs during infection (synpharyngitic); PSGN occurs after a latent period.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Wrong about glomerulonephritis:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Glomerulonephritis characteristically shows haematuria, RBC casts (glomerular bleeding) and dysmorphic RBCs (deformed by passage through the damaged GBM). IgE deposition is NOT a feature — GN involves IgA (IgA nephropathy), IgG (membranous GN) or IgM, not IgE.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Systemic symptoms of acute poststreptococcal GN: 1. Headache  2. Malaise  3. Hematuria  4. Pretibial pitting
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Headache (from hypertension) and malaise are systemic symptoms of PSGN. Haematuria is a urinary/renal manifestation, not a systemic symptom. Pretibial pitting oedema is a clinical sign of volume overload, also not a systemic symptom. Only headache and malaise qualify as systemic.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Seen in acute poststreptococcal GN: 1. Anorexia  2. Proteinuria  3. Flank pain  4. Periorbital edema
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: All four are found in APSGN: anorexia (constitutional), proteinuria (nephritic range, mild-to-moderate), flank pain (capsular stretch from renal swelling) and periorbital oedema (classic early manifestation, especially in children, from sodium and water retention).

Glomerular Diseases.question: What can help confirm the diagnosis of acute poststreptococcal GN?
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Elevated anti-DNase B (and ASO) titers confirm recent Group A β-haemolytic streptococcal infection and support the PSGN diagnosis. Serum C3 is DECREASED in PSGN (complement consumption by immune complexes), not increased. Hypertension and LVH are common but nonspecific.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Increased titers of which antibodies confirm poststreptococcal GN? 1. Antistrepto-DNase  2. Anti-GBM  3. Antiphospholipid  4. Antistreptohyaluronidase
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Antistrepto-DNase B and antistreptohyaluronidase both confirm recent streptococcal infection and support PSGN diagnosis. Anti-GBM antibodies are seen in Goodpasture syndrome; antiphospholipid antibodies in antiphospholipid syndrome — neither is relevant to PSGN.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Causes of hypercoagulation in nephrotic syndrome: 1. Hypofibrinogenemia  2. Urinary loss of antithrombin III  3. Reduced serum protein S  4. Reduced serum protein C
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Hypercoagulability in nephrotic syndrome results from urinary loss of antithrombin III (reduced thrombin inhibition), reduced protein S and protein C (impaired anticoagulant pathways). Fibrinogen is ELEVATED (not reduced) in nephrotic syndrome, contributing further to thrombotic risk.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Podocyte abnormalities with genetic mutations lead to:
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Mutations in podocyte structural/slit-diaphragm proteins (nephrin-NPHS1, podocin-NPHS2, α-actinin-4, TRPC6) cause intrinsic podocyte dysfunction leading to primary (genetic/familial) FSGS with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. Membranous GN is autoimmune (anti-PLA2R), not podocyte mutation–driven.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Treatment of secondary FSGS must include: 1. Glucocorticosteroid  2. Immunosuppressive agent  3. Treatment of underlying cause  4. Control of proteinuria
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Secondary FSGS is structural/adaptive, not immune-mediated. Treatment targets the underlying cause (e.g. stopping pamidronate, treating obesity/reflux) and proteinuria control with ACEi/ARBs. Glucocorticoids and immunosuppressives are not indicated in secondary FSGS.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Which of the following are presented by nephrotic syndrome? 1. Membranous GN  2. Hematuria  3. Diabetic nephropathy  4. Renal amyloidosis
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Membranous GN, diabetic nephropathy and renal amyloidosis all cause heavy glomerular proteinuria leading to nephrotic syndrome. Haematuria is a feature of nephritic syndrome (glomerular inflammation), not of nephrotic syndrome per se.

Glomerular Diseases.question: True about features of FSGS: 1. Hypertension  2. Proteinuria 5.2 g/24 h  3. Proteinuria 4.7 g/24 h  4. Hematuria
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: FSGS characteristically presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria (>3.5 g/day — both 5.2 and 4.7 g/24 h qualify), hypertension (from reduced nephron mass and progressive renal dysfunction) and microscopic haematuria (more common than in minimal change disease). All four features are typical.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Treatment of nephrotic syndrome in renal amyloidosis must include: 1. Complete bed rest  2. Supportive stockings  3. Albumin slow IV infusions  4. Diuretics
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Management is supportive: compression stockings (reduce oedema and thrombotic risk), IV albumin (for refractory oedema in severe hypoalbuminaemia) and loop diuretics (mainstay of oedema control). Complete bed rest is NOT recommended — immobilisation increases thrombotic risk, which is already elevated in nephrotic syndrome.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Causes of transient proteinuria: 1. Fever  2. Exercise  3. Sleep apnea  4. Nephrotic syndrome
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Fever, exercise and sleep apnoea all cause reversible transient proteinuria through haemodynamic or permeability changes. Nephrotic syndrome is characterised by persistent heavy proteinuria from structural glomerular disease — it is not a cause of transient proteinuria.

Glomerular Diseases.question: Causes of transient proteinuria: 1. Obesity  2. Emotional stress  3. Exercise  4. Nephritic syndrome
Glomerular Diseases.explanation: Obesity (hyperfiltration), emotional stress (catecholamine-induced permeability changes) and exercise are recognised causes of transient functional proteinuria. Nephritic syndrome produces persistent proteinuria from glomerular inflammation and is not a cause of transient proteinuria.

Tubulointerstitial Diseases.question: Wrong about chronic pyelonephritis:
options: Most important in treatment is urine passage restoration
Important in treatment is antibiotic administration
Tubulointerstitial Diseases.explanation: Chronic pyelonephritis is a tubulointerstitial disease — it does NOT cause nephrotic syndrome (a glomerular feature). It produces mild proteinuria, tubular dysfunction and progressive CKD. Restoring urine passage, giving antibiotics and acknowledging progression to CKD are all correct statements.

Tubulointerstitial Diseases.question: False about chronic pyelonephritis:
options: Most important in treatment is urine passage restoration
Important in treatment is antibiotic administration
Tubulointerstitial Diseases.explanation: Chronic pyelonephritis is a tubulointerstitial disease causing mild proteinuria, tubular dysfunction and progressive CKD — it does NOT present as nephritic syndrome (a glomerular feature). Restoring urine passage, antibiotics and acknowledging CKD progression are all correct statements.

Tubulointerstitial Diseases.question: Typical for exacerbation of chronic pyelonephritis: 1. Fever  2. Leukocyturia  3. Non-selective proteinuria  4. Cysturia
Tubulointerstitial Diseases.explanation: Fever and leukocyturia (pyuria) are hallmarks of active renal parenchymal infection. Non-selective proteinuria is a glomerular (nephrotic) finding — pyelonephritis causes mild tubular proteinuria. Cystinuria is a hereditary amino acid transport disorder unrelated to pyelonephritis.

Tubulointerstitial Diseases.question: What is NOT typical for chronic pyelonephritis?
Tubulointerstitial Diseases.explanation: Fever, bacteriuria and flank pain (especially in exacerbations) are all typical of chronic pyelonephritis. Nephrotic-range proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) is NOT typical — chronic pyelonephritis causes mild-to-moderate tubular proteinuria; heavy glomerular proteinuria indicates glomerular disease.

Tubulointerstitial Diseases.question: Chronic pyelonephritis — not true:
options: Asymmetrical lesion, calculi, pelvic changes on X-ray
Complete ureteral obstruction is a known etiologic factor
Tubulointerstitial Diseases.explanation: Chronic pyelonephritis leads to CKD (progressive scarring), shows asymmetric scarring/deformed calyces/calculi on imaging, and can be caused by chronic ureteral obstruction. 'Ureteric passage aspiration' is not a recognised treatment — standard management is antibiotics and correction of obstruction or reflux.

Tubulointerstitial Diseases.question: Not typical for exacerbation of chronic pyelonephritis:
Tubulointerstitial Diseases.explanation: Exacerbations of chronic pyelonephritis present with fever, dysuria and leukocyturia (hallmarks of active UTI/renal infection). Massive proteinuria is NOT a feature — pyelonephritis is a tubulointerstitial disease causing mild proteinuria; nephrotic-range proteinuria indicates glomerular disease.

Tubulointerstitial Diseases.question: GCs (glucocorticoids) are indicated in interstitial nephritis — EXCEPT:
Tubulointerstitial Diseases.explanation: Glucocorticoids are indicated for immune-mediated interstitial nephritis: sarcoidosis (granulomatous), Sjögren's syndrome (autoimmune) and TINU syndrome. TB is an infectious cause — primary treatment is antituberculous therapy, and steroids are not routinely indicated.

Tubulointerstitial Diseases.question: GCs indicated in interstitial nephritis — EXCEPT:
Tubulointerstitial Diseases.explanation: SLE, Sjögren's syndrome and sarcoidosis are immune-mediated causes of interstitial nephritis where glucocorticoids are indicated. TB is an infectious cause requiring antituberculous therapy — GCs are not standard treatment.

Tubulointerstitial Diseases.question: Analgesic nephropathy results from: 1. Prednisolone  2. Aspirin + propoxyphene  3. Aspirin + allopurinol  4. Phenacetin + aspirin + caffeine
Tubulointerstitial Diseases.explanation: Analgesic nephropathy (chronic interstitial nephritis and papillary necrosis) is caused by chronic use of combination analgesics: aspirin + propoxyphene and the classic phenacetin + aspirin + caffeine combination. Prednisolone is a corticosteroid with no association; allopurinol treats gout and is not implicated.

Tubulointerstitial Diseases.question: Shedding of necrotic papilla in analgesic nephropathy leads to: 1. Ureteric colic  2. Gross hematuria  3. Nephrotic syndrome  4. Ureteral obstruction
Tubulointerstitial Diseases.explanation: When a necrotic renal papilla detaches, it can cause ureteric colic (colicky flank pain from passage), gross haematuria and ureteral obstruction (if the papilla lodges in the ureter). Nephrotic syndrome is a glomerular feature and does not result from papillary necrosis.

Tubulointerstitial Diseases.question: Causes of chronic tubulointerstitial disorders — EXCEPT:
Tubulointerstitial Diseases.explanation: All four are recognised causes of chronic tubulointerstitial disease: lithium (chronic nephropathy), radiotherapy (radiation nephritis), VUR (chronic pyelonephritis and scarring) and phenacetin/analgesics (analgesic nephropathy). None of these is an exception — all are valid causes.

Tubulointerstitial Diseases.question: Minimal proteinuria is defined as less than:
Tubulointerstitial Diseases.explanation: Minimal (mild) proteinuria is conventionally defined as <500 mg/24 h. Above 500 mg/24 h is considered significant/moderate; nephrotic-range is >3.5 g/24 h.

Amyloidosis.question: Ecchymoses are due to: 1. Uremia  2. AL amyloidosis  3. Aβ amyloidosis  4. Osler's nodes
Amyloidosis.explanation: Uremia causes platelet dysfunction and easy bruising/ecchymoses. AL amyloidosis classically produces periorbital ecchymoses ('raccoon eyes') from amyloid infiltration causing vascular fragility. Aβ amyloidosis is associated with Alzheimer disease (no systemic ecchymoses). Osler's nodes are painful nodules in infective endocarditis, not ecchymoses.

Amyloidosis.question: What is pathognomonic of ATTR amyloidosis?
Amyloidosis.explanation: Vitreous opacities (from local TTR production in the eye) are considered pathognomonic of hereditary ATTR amyloidosis. ATTR also causes peripheral/autonomic neuropathy and cardiomyopathy. Posterior uveitis is not characteristic; splenomegaly is non-specific.

Amyloidosis.question: True about amyloidosis:
Amyloidosis.explanation: Amyloidosis is defined by extracellular deposition of insoluble, misfolded protein fibrils in a β-pleated sheet configuration, showing Congo red positivity and apple-green birefringence under polarised light. Aschoff bodies are seen in rheumatic fever; Janeway lesions in infective endocarditis.

Amyloidosis.question: Typical of AL amyloidosis: 1. Autonomic neuropathy  2. Alopecia  3. Osteophyte formation  4. Easy bruising
Amyloidosis.explanation: AL amyloidosis characteristically causes autonomic neuropathy (orthostatic hypotension, GI dysmotility), alopecia and easy bruising/periorbital purpura (vascular fragility from amyloid infiltration). Osteophyte formation is a feature of osteoarthritis — not AL amyloidosis.

Amyloidosis.question: Aβ2M amyloidosis involves: 1. Carpal tunnel syndrome  2. Bones  3. Synovial membranes  4. Joints
Amyloidosis.explanation: Aβ₂M (dialysis-related) amyloidosis predominantly affects the musculoskeletal system: carpal tunnel syndrome (earliest/most common), bone cysts and pathological fractures, synovial inflammation and chronic arthropathy. All four structures are involved.

Amyloidosis.question: Familial amyloidosis most commonly is due to mutation of:
Amyloidosis.explanation: Transthyretin (TTR) gene mutations are by far the most common cause of familial (hereditary) amyloidosis worldwide, causing peripheral/autonomic neuropathy, cardiomyopathy and vitreous opacities. Fibrinogen causes rare renal-limited hereditary amyloidosis; gelsolin causes Finnish-type familial amyloidosis; calcitonin is associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma.

Amyloidosis.question: 'Raccoon-eyes' symptom is characteristic of …… amyloidosis:
Amyloidosis.explanation: Periorbital ecchymoses ('raccoon eyes') are the classic sign of AL (light-chain) amyloidosis, caused by amyloid infiltration of small vessels producing vascular fragility. Minor trauma (e.g. rubbing the eyes) leads to periorbital purpura. Aβ is Alzheimer-related; AANF and AGE are not causes of this sign.

Amyloidosis.question: Organ involvement in AA amyloidosis usually begins in:
Amyloidosis.explanation: In AA (secondary) amyloidosis, the kidneys are the first and most clinically significant organ involved, presenting with proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome and progressive renal insufficiency. Spleen and liver may also be affected but renal involvement dominates the clinical picture.

Amyloidosis.question: Colchicine at a dose of 1.2–1.8 mg/d is the standard treatment of AA amyloidosis caused by:
Amyloidosis.explanation: Colchicine 1.2–1.8 mg/day is the standard therapy for familial Mediterranean fever (FMF): it suppresses inflammatory attacks, prevents the development of AA amyloidosis and may stabilise or improve established renal involvement. It is not the standard agent for the other listed causes of AA amyloidosis.

Amyloidosis.question: Typical of AL amyloidosis: 1. Osteophytes formation  2. Thickening of synovial membranes  3. Tophi  4. Heberden's nodes
Amyloidosis.explanation: In AL amyloidosis, periarticular amyloid deposition can produce osteophyte-like changes and synovial thickening/arthropathy. Tophi are urate crystal deposits seen in gout; Heberden's nodes are bony prominences of osteoarthritis — neither is caused by amyloidosis.

Amyloidosis.question: Typical of AL amyloidosis: 1. Neuropathy  2. Alopecia  3. Osteophytes formation  4. Thickening of synovial membranes
Amyloidosis.explanation: AL amyloidosis causes peripheral/autonomic neuropathy, alopecia, osteophyte-like periarticular changes and synovial thickening/arthropathy from amyloid infiltration. All four are recognised manifestations.

Amyloidosis.question: Aβ2M amyloidosis presents with: 1. Carpal tunnel syndrome  2. Alzheimer's disease  3. Spondyloarthropathy  4. Cystic bone lesions
Amyloidosis.explanation: Aβ₂M (dialysis-related) amyloidosis affects the musculoskeletal system: carpal tunnel syndrome (earliest manifestation), destructive spondyloarthropathy and cystic bone lesions. Alzheimer's disease is associated with Aβ (amyloid-beta) — a completely different protein.

Amyloidosis.question: Aβ2M amyloidosis presents with: 1. Carpal tunnel syndrome  2. Cystic bone lesions  3. Spondyloarthropathy  4. Persistent joint effusions
Amyloidosis.explanation: All four are typical of Aβ₂M (dialysis-related) amyloidosis: carpal tunnel syndrome, cystic bone lesions (risk of pathological fractures), destructive spondyloarthropathy and persistent joint effusions from synovial amyloid infiltration.

Amyloidosis.question: Characteristic in progressed AA amyloidosis: 1. Hepatomegaly  2. Splenomegaly  3. Autonomic neuropathy  4. Nephrotic syndrome
Amyloidosis.explanation: In advanced AA amyloidosis: hepatomegaly and splenomegaly ('sago/lardaceous spleen') from organ infiltration, autonomic neuropathy (more typical of AL/ATTR but occurs in advanced systemic AA), and nephrotic syndrome (the earliest and most prominent renal manifestation). All four can be present.

Amyloidosis.question: Wrong about renal amyloidosis: 1. Unilateral affection  2. Bilateral affection  3. Calyceal-pelvic deformity  4. Kidneys are rarely involved in AL amyloidosis
Amyloidosis.explanation: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are wrong: renal amyloidosis is bilateral (not unilateral); calyceal-pelvic deformity is characteristic of chronic pyelonephritis, not amyloidosis; kidneys are commonly (not rarely) involved in AL amyloidosis, often presenting with nephrotic syndrome. Statement 2 (bilateral affection) is correct.

Amyloidosis.question: Liver transplantation can slow progression of …… amyloidosis:
Amyloidosis.explanation: Mutant transthyretin (TTR) is primarily produced by the liver. In hereditary ATTR amyloidosis, liver transplantation removes the source of mutant TTR, reducing further amyloid deposition and slowing disease progression (especially neuropathic forms). TTR stabilisers (tafamidis) are now also available.

Amyloidosis.question: More frequently affected joints in Aβ₂M amyloidosis: 1. Shoulders  2. Knees  3. Wrists  4. Hips
Amyloidosis.explanation: Dialysis-related (Aβ₂M) amyloidosis preferentially deposits in synovium and periarticular structures of large joints. All four — shoulders, knees, wrists (associated with carpal tunnel syndrome) and hips — are commonly affected.

Amyloidosis.question: True about amyloidosis: 1. Extracellular deposition  2. Intracellular deposition  3. Insoluble polymeric protein fibrils  4. Soluble polymeric protein fibrils
Amyloidosis.explanation: Amyloidosis is defined by extracellular deposition of insoluble, misfolded protein fibrils in a β-pleated sheet configuration (Congo red-positive, apple-green birefringence). Deposition is extracellular (not intracellular) and the fibrils are insoluble (not soluble).

Amyloidosis.question: Which is true for Aβ₂M amyloidosis — EXCEPT:
Amyloidosis.explanation: Aβ₂M amyloidosis is caused by β₂-microglobulin accumulation in long-term dialysis patients and causes cystic bone lesions, destructive spondyloarthropathy and carpal tunnel syndrome. Gout (monosodium urate crystal deposition) is a completely separate condition unrelated to amyloidosis.

Amyloidosis.question: Renal amyloidosis — EXCEPT: 1. Unilateral affection  2. ↓ Size of kidney  3. Proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome  4. Wilson's nodules
Amyloidosis.explanation: Items 1, 2 and 4 are incorrect about renal amyloidosis: it is bilateral (not unilateral); kidneys are usually normal or enlarged (not small); Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules are characteristic of diabetic nephropathy, not amyloidosis. Proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome are correct — they are typical features.

Amyloidosis.question: Causes of AA amyloidosis — EXCEPT:
Amyloidosis.explanation: AA amyloidosis results from chronic elevation of serum amyloid A in persistent inflammatory or infectious states: Crohn's disease, TB and subacute endocarditis all qualify. Osteoarthritis is a degenerative (non-inflammatory) joint disease and is NOT associated with AA amyloidosis.

Amyloidosis.question: Secondary (AA) amyloidosis is present in: 1. Rheumatoid arthritis  2. Myeloma  3. Bronchiectasis  4. Osteomyelitis
Amyloidosis.explanation: AA amyloidosis occurs in chronic inflammatory and infectious conditions: rheumatoid arthritis (most common cause), bronchiectasis (chronic suppurative lung disease) and osteomyelitis (chronic infection). Myeloma causes AL amyloidosis (immunoglobulin light chains), not AA amyloidosis.

Amyloidosis.question: Characteristic of AL amyloidosis — TRUE: 1. Diarrhea  2. Constipation  3. Early satiety  4. Autonomic dysfunction → orthostatic hypotension
Amyloidosis.explanation: All four are true of AL amyloidosis: diarrhoea and constipation (autonomic neuropathy and intestinal amyloid infiltration), early satiety (gastric infiltration or gastroparesis from autonomic neuropathy) and orthostatic hypotension (classic autonomic dysfunction from amyloid in autonomic nerves).

Amyloidosis.question: AA amyloidosis causes: 1. Subacute bacterial endocarditis  2. Familial Mediterranean fever  3. Ulcerative colitis  4. Rheumatoid arthritis
Amyloidosis.explanation: All four are causes of AA amyloidosis: subacute bacterial endocarditis (chronic infection), FMF (recurrent inflammatory attacks — classic cause), ulcerative colitis (chronic IBD inflammation) and rheumatoid arthritis (one of the most common causes globally).

Amyloidosis.question: In violet-colored periorbital rash — which disease?
Amyloidosis.explanation: A violet (heliotrope) periorbital rash is pathognomonic of dermatomyositis. It presents as violaceous discolouration on the upper eyelids with periorbital oedema. AL amyloidosis causes periorbital ecchymoses ('raccoon eyes'), which are purplish but due to vascular fragility rather than the heliotrope rash.

Amyloidosis.question: Seen in AL amyloidosis: 1. Nail dystrophy  2. Alopecia  3. Osteophytes formation  4. Thickening of synovial membranes
Amyloidosis.explanation: AL amyloidosis causes nail dystrophy (amyloid in dermis/nails), alopecia (skin involvement) and synovial thickening/arthropathy (amyloid in joints). Osteophyte formation is a feature of osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), NOT amyloidosis.

Amyloidosis.question: Seen in AL amyloidosis: 1. Weight loss  2. Autonomic neuropathy  3. Alzheimer's disease  4. Macroglossia
Amyloidosis.explanation: AL amyloidosis causes weight loss (constitutional), autonomic neuropathy (orthostatic hypotension, GI dysmotility) and macroglossia (classic — amyloid infiltration of tongue). Alzheimer's disease involves cerebral Aβ amyloid — a completely different protein and pathological process from AL amyloidosis.

Amyloidosis.question: Seen in AL amyloidosis: 1. Early satiety  2. Nail dystrophy  3. Orthostatic hypotension  4. Easy bruising
Amyloidosis.explanation: All four are features of AL amyloidosis: early satiety (GI infiltration/gastroparesis), nail dystrophy (skin/nail amyloid), orthostatic hypotension (autonomic neuropathy) and easy bruising (vascular fragility from amyloid in vessel walls and possible factor X deficiency).

Amyloidosis.question: Causes of AA amyloidosis — EXCEPT:
Amyloidosis.explanation: AA amyloidosis results from sustained elevation of serum amyloid A in chronic inflammation or infection: subacute bacterial endocarditis, FMF and TB are all chronic conditions that qualify. Myocardial infarction is an acute event that does not cause sustained SAA elevation sufficient to produce AA amyloidosis.

UTI and Pyelonephritis.question: Which of the following is the diagnostic 'gold standard' for UTI? Detection of …… in urine culture:
UTI and Pyelonephritis.explanation: The gold standard for UTI diagnosis is urine culture demonstrating bacteria (identifying the causative organism, quantifying CFU/mL and guiding antibiotic sensitivity). RBCs suggest glomerular disease; dysmorphic RBCs suggest glomerulonephritis; pyuria (WBCs) supports but does not confirm UTI without bacteriuria.

UTI and Pyelonephritis.question: Patients with cystitis present with: 1. Dysuria  2. Suprapubic pain  3. Frequency  4. Urgency
UTI and Pyelonephritis.explanation: Acute cystitis classically presents with the full quartet: dysuria (hallmark burning on micturition), suprapubic pain (bladder inflammation), frequency and urgency. All four together form the classic presentation of uncomplicated lower UTI.

UTI and Pyelonephritis.question: Cause of acute hemorrhagic cystitis in young adults:
UTI and Pyelonephritis.explanation: Adenovirus (particularly types 11 and 21) is the classic cause of acute haemorrhagic cystitis in young adults and children, presenting with gross haematuria, dysuria and frequency in a self-limited course. Ureaplasma and Mycoplasma cause urethritis; Candida cystitis is seen in immunocompromised or catheterised patients.

UTI and Pyelonephritis.question: All of the following fluoroquinolones are commonly used for UTI treatment, except one:
UTI and Pyelonephritis.explanation: Ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin and levofloxacin all achieve adequate urinary concentrations and are used for UTI treatment. Moxifloxacin is the exception — it achieves poor urinary concentrations and is used primarily for respiratory infections, not UTIs.

UTI and Pyelonephritis.question: Seen in acute pyelonephritis: 1. Chills  2. Fever  3. Hypoalbuminemia  4. Nausea
UTI and Pyelonephritis.explanation: Acute pyelonephritis presents with chills, high fever (systemic inflammatory response) and nausea/vomiting. Hypoalbuminaemia is not a feature — it is characteristic of nephrotic syndrome or chronic illness, not acute bacterial renal infection.

UTI and Pyelonephritis.question: A 74-year-old woman has a UTI. Which is the most likely coexisting condition?
UTI and Pyelonephritis.explanation: Diabetes mellitus is the most common predisposing condition for UTI in elderly women, due to impaired neutrophil function, autonomic neuropathy causing incomplete bladder emptying, glycosuria promoting bacterial growth and increased risk of complicated/recurrent infections. Anaemia, analgesic use and exercise are not recognised UTI risk factors.

UTI and Pyelonephritis.question: Patients with cystitis present with: 1. Dysuria and suprapubic pain  2. Pruritus  3. Frequency  4. Urgency
UTI and Pyelonephritis.explanation: Acute cystitis classically presents with dysuria/suprapubic pain, urinary frequency and urgency. Pruritus is more suggestive of vaginitis or vulvovaginal infection, not cystitis.

UTI and Pyelonephritis.question: Seen in acute pyelonephritis: 1. Chills  2. Fever  3. Feet edema  4. Nausea
UTI and Pyelonephritis.explanation: Acute pyelonephritis presents with chills (from bacteraemia and systemic inflammation), high fever and nausea/vomiting. Peripheral oedema (feet) is not a feature — it is more associated with nephrotic syndrome, heart failure or chronic renal disease.

UTI and Pyelonephritis.question: Severe pyelonephritis presents with: 1. Fever  2. Rigors  3. Flank pain  4. Nausea/vomiting
UTI and Pyelonephritis.explanation: All four are characteristic of severe acute pyelonephritis: fever and rigors (systemic inflammatory response/bacteraemia), flank pain (renal capsular inflammation) and nausea/vomiting (systemic illness). Together these form the classic clinical triad of upper UTI.

Diabetic Nephropathy.question: Morphologic change appears in kidney — how many years after clinical appearance of diabetes?
Diabetic Nephropathy.explanation: In diabetic nephropathy, functional changes (hyperfiltration, microalbuminuria) precede structural ones. Morphologic changes (mesangial expansion, GBM thickening, Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules) become clearly demonstrable approximately 10 years after the clinical onset of diabetes, particularly in type 1 DM.

Diabetic Nephropathy.question: Microalbuminuria is a risk factor for:
Diabetic Nephropathy.explanation: Microalbuminuria (30–300 mg albumin/24 h) is a marker of generalised endothelial dysfunction and vascular injury. It is strongly and independently associated with increased cardiovascular disease risk (MI, stroke, cardiovascular mortality), not pulmonary or respiratory conditions.

Diabetic Nephropathy.question: In patients with Type 1/Type 2 DM — after how many years of clinical disease does microalbuminuria typically appear?
Diabetic Nephropathy.explanation: In type 1 DM, microalbuminuria typically develops after 5–10 years of clinically evident disease. In type 2 DM it may be present at diagnosis (due to years of undetected hyperglycaemia) but classically also appears after several years of disease.

Diabetic Nephropathy.question: Risk factors for diabetic nephropathy: 1. Hyperglycemia  2. Hypoglycemia  3. Hypertension  4. Dyslipidemia
Diabetic Nephropathy.explanation: Hyperglycaemia (primary driver of glomerular injury), hypertension (accelerates progression via intraglomerular hypertension) and dyslipidaemia (contributes to glomerular injury) are the major modifiable risk factors for diabetic nephropathy. Hypoglycaemia is not a risk factor.

Diabetic Nephropathy.question: Risk factors for diabetic nephropathy: 1. Hyperglycemia  2. Hypercholesterolemia  3. Hypertension  4. Dyslipidemia
Diabetic Nephropathy.explanation: All four are recognised risk factors: hyperglycaemia (primary driver), hypercholesterolaemia and dyslipidaemia (contribute to vascular and glomerular injury) and hypertension (major independent accelerator of nephropathy progression).

Diabetic Nephropathy.question: Cause of albuminuria in Type 2 DM — which is an unrelated secondary factor?
Diabetic Nephropathy.explanation: Severe hypertension (hypertensive nephrosclerosis), CCF (renal venous congestion) and infection (UTI causing transient albuminuria) can all independently cause albuminuria in T2DM. Prostatic disease causes urinary obstruction and infection risk but is not a direct independent cause of albuminuria.

Diabetic Nephropathy.question: Management of albuminuria/diabetic nephropathy includes: 1. Glycemic control  2. Diuretics  3. ACE inhibitors  4. ARBs
Diabetic Nephropathy.explanation: Glycaemic control, ACE inhibitors and ARBs (not combined) are cornerstones of treatment: they reduce intraglomerular pressure, decrease albuminuria and slow CKD progression even in normotensive patients. Diuretics help control BP/oedema but do not independently slow albuminuria progression.

Diabetic Nephropathy.question: Non-diabetic albuminuria — related conditions include: 1. Severe HTN  2. CCF  3. Vigorous exercise  4. Chronic pyelonephritis
Diabetic Nephropathy.explanation: All four can cause non-diabetic albuminuria: hypertensive nephrosclerosis, renal venous congestion from CCF, transient functional albuminuria from vigorous exercise, and mild-to-moderate albuminuria from tubulointerstitial damage in chronic pyelonephritis.

Diabetic Nephropathy.question: Interventions that slow progression from microalbuminuria to macroalbuminuria: 1. Glycemic control  2. Diuretics  3. ACE inhibitors  4. Systemic hypertension treatment
Diabetic Nephropathy.explanation: Glycaemic control, ACE inhibitors (reduce intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria) and blood pressure treatment all significantly slow progression of albuminuria in diabetic nephropathy. Diuretics alone do not independently slow albuminuria progression.

Diabetic Nephropathy.question: All are typical in advanced diabetic nephropathy, except:
Diabetic Nephropathy.explanation: Advanced diabetic nephropathy shows persistent proteinuria, normal-to-enlarged kidneys (unlike most other CKD where kidneys shrink) and Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodular glomerulosclerosis on biopsy. Small shrunken kidneys are typical of other chronic kidney diseases but NOT diabetic nephropathy until very late stages.

Diabetic Nephropathy.question: In DM — pathological change in kidney includes: 1. Fibrosis  2. Nephrosclerosis  3. Insulin/growth factor activation  4. Fibroblast activation
Diabetic Nephropathy.explanation: All four are pathological changes in diabetic nephropathy: progressive fibrosis, glomerulosclerosis/nephrosclerosis (including Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules), growth factor activation (particularly TGF-β and IGF) driving mesangial expansion and matrix deposition, and fibroblast stimulation contributing to interstitial fibrosis.

Menstrual Disorders.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with heavy, irregular menstrual bleeding for 8 months. Examination and USS are normal. Endometrial biopsy shows no pathology. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Menstrual Disorders.explanation: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB) is a diagnosis of exclusion — abnormal uterine bleeding with no identifiable structural or systemic cause. Normal USS and biopsy with no pathology confirms DUB, most commonly due to anovulatory cycles.
